name: Yellow Grey
lede: Yellow grey is a descriptive name for a dull, drab green-yellow-grey, the color of string, and in paintings often a hidden color.

sections.title: A drab with a name hunt
sections.body:
Yellow grey is a description: a grey tinted with yellow [1]. Paterson uses the words to define two older names. String is a light beige-brown or yellow-grey, and isabel or isabella is a dingy yellow grey [1]. The story often told for isabella, that it recalls an archduchess who wore the same underclothes for years, is a legend, and Paterson notes more than one candidate for the lady [1].

St Clair observes that a shopper looking for pale yellow-grays will not find one actually called beige, a word she suggests marketers shy away from for its sound [2]. A close cousin is [[khaki]]: the word does not come from the French name for the persimmon, *kaki*, but from a Hindustani word meaning earth or dust colour [3]. [[taupe]] and [[olive-green]] sit nearby.

sections.title: The yellow-grey of age
sections.body: The color is also a sign of change. Ball describes a rare fault in ultramarine paint, the so-called sickness, where blue turns patchy and greyish or yellow-grey, for reasons still not fully understood [4]. Yellowing varnish, soiled ground and dulled paint all push painted surfaces toward this tone, which may be one reason it is so common in our measurements [5].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Yellow grey appears in 8.69% of the 23,781 paintings in our archive, 2,067 paintings, as photographed, which makes it more common than 93% of the named colors [5]. Inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color, in 44% of the 1,312 paintings where we measure roles [5].

It peaks in the 1900s, at 7.5% of the 1,674 paintings from then, 1.5x the baseline of the same museums [5]. Johannes Lingelbach is the painter most devoted to it, with the color in 7 of 16 works here [5]. The earliest match, 916, is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, 1,011 years before the name's earliest record in our sources, the 1927 RAL list [5]. It shares canvases more than chance with Yellowish Glaucous and Old bamboo [5].
